items.body:
Enigmatic audity Aisie returns five years on from a strange, overlooked debut with a new suite of compressed atmospheres highly tipped FFO False Aralia, Eliza B.C., Thought Broadcast, Civilistjävel!, Hazyville-era Actress.

‘Black Fire Dream’ picks up from where 2021’s ‘Halcyon Gang Poet’ left us in a surreal, uncanny valley state of mind. The seven part, 30 minute mini-LP continues to fascinate with its cyborganic nature and dreamy otherworldliness, luring down gauzily textured, fractal wormholes where samples of “obscure educational science shows, ghost station radio transmissions, vinyl record detritus and blown-out microscopic field recordings” are gently reanimated and transmuted with a poetic sorcery. 

The whole thing feels as though it were conjuured without human touch, like the inner thoughts of an AI or machines autonomously air-syncing and executing their functions in private. With incremental stealth it breezes by in a hypnagogic haze, half-heard melodies sprouting and dissolving into the aether as granular rhythms buckle and trickle. Eyes will likely be at half mast by the end of the A-side, all the best to receive the B-side’s suggestive, illusive shadowplay of smoke and mirrors refraction and a final slope off into something like a chopped and screwed echo of Topdown Dialectic.

items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."

items.body:
Showcasing contemporary Algerian sounds led by the gasba, a traditional reeded flute, 'My Heart is Dust Before Him' is a collaboration between Hive Mind and Oran's Édition Ahlem imprint.

In the Berber language, "gaspa" means "reed", and references the wind instrument that's central to some of the region's most gripping Bedouin folk and ceremonial music. On this 10-track anthology, Hive Mind plucks tracks from Édition Ahlem's recent catalogue; the label emerged in Oran from a record store and puts out cassettes since the early '90s. These selections are a little more contemporary and examine how the gasba forms have mutated and evolved in the last couple of decades, reacting to production changes while retaining the unique sound of the flute itself.

There's plenty to explore here, from the dimly lit distortions of Cheikh Tahar Oueld Marhoum's 'Naachak Fiha Ou Magoulhach' and Cheba Negouane's rai-adjacent 'Ychafouni Maghbounat' to Cheikh El Waal's woozy organ-led 'El Galb Maamar' and Mohamed Ain Larbaa's unexpectedly funky 'Sratli Khatra Kheleft L3ahed'.

items.body:
Necessary reissue of Marc Leclair’s immaculate Y2K micro-house/dub-house 12” as Akufen, dispensed by Low End Activist’s guess-again BRUK sibling to Sneaker Social Club - huge RIYL Maurizio, Studio 1, Mike Huckaby.

‘Architextures 1 -2 -3’ is a sought-after slice of hypnotic house by a noted pioneer of the micro-house movement that emerged in the late ‘90s. Its reissue arrives in the wake of a re-up for Marc Leclair’s (aka Akufen) sole solo album ‘Musique Pour 3 Femmes Enceintes’ (2005) with a strong reminder of his pivotal role in dressing house music down to fundamentals around the millennium, as deployed in Richie Hawtin mixes and praised for its exquisitely efficient, effortless, hiccuping funk.

It’s really all about the  A-side’s ‘Architexture 1’, a pendulous 127BPM roller inflected with chef’s kiss dub chords and frisky drums, on one of the smoothest, deepest basslines since ‘M5’. There’s a good reason why it’s been fetching triple figures on 2nd hand markets, so BRUK are doing the Lord’s work with this reissue, which also includes the slower, sub-heavier swivel of its Pt. 2, and more signature, strutting clip of his tight sampling tekkerz on Pt. 3.

TIP!

items.body:
Limited edition, first time 2LP re-issue of a compilation originally released via Gary Mundy's legendary Broken Flag imprint in 1987 and featuring a veritable who’s who of post industrial drone and psyche/power electronics including Ramleh, Total, Andrew Chalk and many more.​

"Remastered by Puppy38, this features two bonus tracks not included on the original (and long o/p) LP but only previously found on the even rarer cassette and the equally o/p CD. A timely reminder of this fantastic archive document full of boundary-pushing artists mostly still active in one form or another. Packaged in a sleeve faithful to the distinctive original Cranioclast-designed cover."

items.excerpt: Left: P+D 02 01 02 (2024); Right: M P Landis & Michael Sarin, May 18, 2024 at L/A Arts, Lewiston, ME Adjacent to a drumkit, two large boards hang above a stage clad in drop cloth. items.body: Left: P+D 02 01 02 (2024); Right: M P Landis & Michael Sarin, May 18, 2024 at L/A Arts, Lewiston, ME Adjacent to a drumkit, two large boards hang above a stage clad in drop cloth. A third lies flat on a small table surrounded by paint bottles and upturned pot lids that will become ad hoc palettes. Each board is covered in paper and divided into grids by white painter's tape: the small board into nine squares and the larger two into twelve. It's the end of June 2026 at the Apohadion Theater in Portland, Maine. Just ahead, the fifth meeting of painter M P Landis and drummer Michael Sarin in a collaboration they've come to call, concisely, Paint & Drums. Fans of creative music may recognize Landis's paintings from the album covers of artists like Flow Trio , [ism] , and Sabir Mateen . His work is part of an estuary somewhere far downstream of the Abstract Expressionists: gestures that range from child-like markings to purposive strokes that convey the whole body's movement; textured clots and layers of color; obscure figures and shapes that could be letters or symbols but offer a mute refusal. But Landis will say he feels less affinity with other visual artists than he does with musicians. Indeed, what stands out about Landis's work is how deeply committed his methods are to the same reactive, exuberant ethos that drives the free improvisers. Music—especially jazz and improvised music—has long been part of Landis's work, both in the studio and in a live setting. In a 2006 conversation with the writer Fred Schmalz, he described arriving at a point in the 1990s where he began using music "as a jumping off point to get beyond my ideas and find a way of working that transcends technique and becomes more emotional and dance-like." Joe Maneri/Mat Maneri/Randy Peterson #1 - #4 (2001). Created live at the 2001 Vision Festival, NYC His career in the decades since validates Mike Heffley's musing in Northern Sun, Southern Moon. "If one were a painter," Heffley wrote, free improvisation "is music that might be the most fruitful aid and stimulus to the process. It encourages one to get physical with one's tools and media, to delight in them as ends in themselves, whatever means they might develop into therefrom." Talking with Schmalz, Landis describes exactly that: "I feel almost like the music uses me or, I guess I use the music to use me. There is a certain surrendering to what I am listening to which helps me jump right into physically moving; making marks, grabbing paint, etc. It overcomes the endless problems of decision and throws me right into the act of creating." Some of Landis's paintings bear titles that pay tribute to the music he was listening to as he painted. But music's influence is more deeply seated. Top: David S. Ware: Onecept triptych (mp13.01, mp13.02, mp13.03) (2013) Bottom Left: PIANO SKY (JOE MANERI) (2003); Bottom Right: lp13.06 (derek bailey) (2013) Landis moved from painting on street corners and in the audience at concerts to frequently painting on stage in collaboration with musicians, dancers, and other visual artists in the vibrant Brooklyn arts scene. He remains a prolific collaborator. The live performances of that period culminated in a tour with the Jump Arts American Road Project in 2002, Landis taking the stage with poet Steve Dalachinsky, dancers, and musicians like Tom Abbs, Daniel Carter, Steve Swell, and Okkyung Lee. Cisco Bradley's recounting of the tour in The Williamsburg Avant-Garde touches on Landis's intense engagement with his materials and an approach to live painting that's still present in Paint & Drums: "[Landis] would paint through the entire evening of performances, with two wooden panels covered in paper on which to work. One panel was covered by one large piece of paper, while the other panel had multiple smaller pieces stapled to it. Landis described his process: 'I painted the whole board, not thinking about where one piece of paper stopped or started. I liked how it gave the work a sense of being midstream, like capturing a sound in time.' He added, 'The intensity of the music made the painting intense. It felt like I was doing months' worth of painting within a few hours.'" Left: american road project 1L (2002); Right: j.a.a.r.p. [#12.] (2002) It was during his time in NYC that Landis met Sarin, then drumming in the storied Thomas Chapin Trio (just one facet of his deep and continued embeddedness in the New York avant-garde). Nearly two decades later, Sarin lamented that he never had a chance to see Landis paint in a live setting and asked if he'd be willing to collaborate. Two performances were arranged in May 2024, and the duo have now met three more times in 2026. A Visual Musician There's an enticing trap, or at least a long stroll to a dead end, in approaching the relationship between Landis's paintings and free jazz. It is to interpret them as somehow "representing" the music. Landis is clear on this: "I don’t mean for [the music] to define the work because I’m not interested in making visual representations of music, or anything for that matter. These paintings and drawings are artifacts of a creative process; a recording of my reactions to not just music, but to life and my living it." Establishing that the relationship is indirect, two smaller traps await, both common responses to abstract music and painting. Treading carefully between them, I'm likely to get a foot caught in each. The first comes from the dismissive "Even I Could Have Done That" school of art criticism; the other adopts a transcendental tone that inflates the abstract nature of these artforms until they're lofted into the clouds. Something like "overwhelming directness" versus "overweening mystery," to borrow from Stanley Cavell. Left to Right: MONK 3. THINK OF ONE (2005); MONK 4. HACKENSACK (2005); MONK 5. 'ROUND MIDNIGHT (2005) The first response is an almost defensive tensing in the face of such directness. A move to immediately let the air out before the overweeners get too jazzed up. "I get it. Your painting is like free jazz: random and improvised and spontaneous." Nothing enigmatic here. You don't really have to know anything, you just have to do. Splatter the paint, whack the drum, toot the horn. This attitude tends to badly underestimate the skill that's required to achieve the allegedly facile result, but there's something perceived here, a focus on the plain fact of bodies in action, that can't be entirely dismissed. The process, the doing, is integral—it's what's insisted by these artforms, what we can always sense even when we try (willfully or otherwise) to bracket it out. In viewing pieces like the "Monk Work" paintings, those initial impressions of sheer spontaneity belie the fact that, just as in lots of jazz and improvised music, accumulated experience and an incredible depth of consideration are channeled into an application of skill, shaping an ongoing process that didn't have a specific end in mind when things got underway. What get overlooked are all the particularities: the whorl of circumstance, body, and action that actually birthed that painting or moment of music. Landis's painting isn't merely like free jazz because both can be loud and break rules. Many of his pieces represent a series of events and decisions through time—sometimes over weeks and months—that are fervently attuned to intention and accident and their intertwining. Left : 16.35T (2016); Right : 19.155 (2019) We often fall back on visual metaphors when trying to talk about music, but the counterintuitive thing about Landis's paintings is that their material likeness to music is not visual, but temporal: they are "impossible" images that inscribe action-through-time in the same way that music does as it plays out. This sense of movement-across-time leaps from their surfaces. Looking at a piece like 16.35T , I really do find myself reaching for musical concepts: there's a staccato rhythm to the marks, which have a lively motion in their stacks of contrapuntal bands. There's dissonance in the dabs of glowing green, which seem to punctuate moments in the painting's development. The paintings have no telos, just as improvised music isn't about getting to the end of playing. They aren't planned and realized ends or even a representation of an instant or "the now" but rather they are a holding-open, a paradoxical attempt to spatialize temporality, or express it all at once. The time-taking is the work in the way music is the running of the clock. This temporal nature is never more apparent than during live performance. There, we see the changing cadences of painting, the transformation of color and form as new strokes merge with old, the accumulation of layers that continually supplant the painting's character, even as glimpses of its previous features remain. Brice Marden once said of Jackson Pollock, "He doesn't apply the image; he lets the image evolve out of the activity." Landis: "I like to push what I make ‘til it feels right, in some inner logic kind of way, even when that leads me to something that might look off or clumsy, but in a way that attracts me." All of these evolved and evolving particularities are exactly why just anyone couldn't create that painting or improvise those sounds. Those unrepeatable elements in concert with the artist's grappling are what constitute the work. If such painting or music could be said to have "content," this is all it could possibly be, and encrypted. You may be physically capable of executing the work, but you could never be existentially capable—you have no access to its means of creation. Top, Left to Right: wd3060 (2006); wd2034 (2004); wd5625 (2013) Middle, Left to Right: wd5921 (2014); wd6016 (2014); wd6058 (2014) Bottom, Left to Right: wd6831 (2016); wd7972 (2019); wd6562 (2016) This idea of paintings as ledgers or accretions of activity is hyper-concentrated in the wd series ("warehouse drawings"). Landis produced 10,000 wd pieces in the nearly thirty years between October 1996 and March 2025. Nearly all began as a folded piece of paper that Landis would carry with him throughout the day, often marked with notes, reminders, shopping lists. "Later in the studio, I chronologically staple them to boards, usually working on 20 at a time, drawing and painting on them, often in multiple layers over many days, weeks and sometimes months in response to whatever is happening in my world at each session." Like a recording of an improvised performance, the wd paintings are the record of happenings that can't ever be restaged, a ledger of events that could never be repeated exactly so. Their accumulation of texture, their creases and sometimes ragged edges, are evidence of their travel through the real world, are the grounding reminders that, however abstract the visuals, they are the products of a creative drive that is selfsame with Landis, moving through life. Though Landis has retired the wd series, hints of their methodology have emerged in a new FP series created on small pieces of folded hand-made paper. Left to Right: FP26.78 (2026); FP26.103 (2026); FP26.174 (2026) Paintings from the wd series often made their way back to music, and the influence began running in the opposite direction. Several have been used as album art, and over the years musicians would ask Landis if they could use a painting as inspiration for music. Most notably, Loren Connors and Suzanne Langille took a number of wd pieces and projected them in the studio while recording, which was subsequently released as I Wish I Didn't Dream . During the pandemic, Landis began a series of smaller, heavily contingent paintings called "Notes." Each month, he starts dozens, which he lays around the house or beneath paintings in the studio, allowing them to gather stains and marks of daily life. "Notes" can be shuffled and combined into larger pieces called "Compositions," forming the basis of graphic scores. In 2024, the Cannery in Penobscot, Maine staged a series of concerts in which "Compositions" were performed by musicians like E. Jason Gibbs, Phillip Greenlief, Leslie Ross, Steve Norton, Laura Cromwell, and others. Top, Left to Right: Note 138 (2020); Note 126 (2020); Note 154 (2020); Note 1131 (2026) Bottom, Left to Right: Note 964 (2025); Note 1121 (2026); Note 1 (2020); Note 702 (2023) Accepting that there's something more than brute, unskilled doing behind such vast and varied artistic output, the "overweening" approach—a propensity I admit I must actively temper—starts from trying to articulate the interesting whatness of all those coalesced particularities . But it can be quick to flight and risks overstating its case. In seeking some ultimate source for often dumbfounding glimpses into a pure creative stream, it also risks leaving the artist behind entirely. Firebrand critic Robert Hughes famously had little patience for this. He once wrote that all of the "verbose obeisances to the Ineffable" in discussions of Mark Rothko's work tended "to be coercive, because of a deep uncertainty about the nature of his art." (I'm not sure what Hughes would make of something like Paint & Drums, though I can imagine him satisfied, standing before the large paintings at the end of the show, still gleaming and dripping.) Hughes's warning is not unfounded, but it's also dismissive of the role uncertainty and small-i ineffability play in the experience of art like Landis's (or Rothko's, for that matter). We find the ineffable creeping up not because this sort of art is a direct mainline to the transcendent Godhead or a manifestation of universal Truth, but because it carries the possibility of ringing within us some deeply sympathetic tone, a personal and close-feeling resonance that never quite carries through into words. This isn't absolute or guaranteed. In truth, it is fleeting and infrequent. But we each know our own private tone and we hope in our encounters to feel that vibration. Returning to Cavell, in "Music Discomposed" he says these kinds of art are " known by feeling , or in feeling," and this underlies our anxiety and difficulty in communicating this knowledge: "I want to tell you something I've seen, or heard, or realized, or come to understand, for the reasons for which such things are communicated (because it is news, about a world we share, or could). Only I find that I can't tell you; and that makes it all the more urgent to tell you. I want to tell you because the knowledge, unshared, is a burden . . . It matters, there is a burden, because unless I can tell you what I know, there is a suggestion (and to myself as well) that I do not know." This uncertainty is not a defect. It is an essential component of the improvised musical set, and of Landis's practice as he steps into his studio each day and faces dozens of paintings in various stages. And, Hughes's self-certainty aside, I think it is also the essential, brightly dark core of our aesthetic experience of these works. It's the same doubt the skeptic amplifies until it distorts into nothingness, easy to dismiss. Uncertainty—not-quite-knowing—is the grip that pulls the artist into the stream, and it's also the grip that gets us by the collar and stops us, to look or to listen. Picking up a paint brush or a saxophone are also attempts to convey news about a world we share, or could. Left: 15.14 (2015); Right: 20.03 (2020) "Somehow Precise, Intense, and Vague All at Once" The heading is Michael Gallope's description of what he calls music's "affective inconsistency," but it also beautifully captures Landis's paintings and the particular energy of his live collaboration with Sarin. One of the more charming aspects of Landis's and Sarin's partnership is that they still aren't quite sure of it. Each time, they gently ease into a start and there's always some hesitation about whether they've finished. This thread of uncertainty runs through the whole performance, is what fuels the excitement, but it also feels more palpable than during a musical improvisation. Left: M P Landis and Michael Sarin, May 15, 2024 at the Apohadion Theater, Portland, ME Top Right: P+D 04 01 03 (2026); Bottom Right: P+D 03 02 02 (2026) In the audience, witnessing the real-time change in the paintings draws out tensions between arising aesthetic judgments and a curiosity about what continuing will yield. As elements emerge in the paintings, there are times when things "feel" finished, or where particular sections or forms satisfy some personal preference. I find myself becoming protective, secretly wishing that further actions will spare a notable swirl of black or a blaze of orange that still burns though layer after layer. I wasn't alone. At several of the performances, others talked about fearing a painting was "ruined" at points during the show, feeling satisfied with a certain stage of the process and forgetting that the process must continue, that the painting in the moment they esteemed it also arose by that process. After the April 2026 performance, one enthusiastic young audience member bantered with Landis about the range of emotions he felt during the show: "At one point, I actually felt angry with you, man! I thought you fucked it up!" Imagining how you think someone should be behaving toward certain sounds or stimuli also leads to subverted expectations. I wonder if the way Landis is moving should be more . . . what? Theatrical? Synchronized? Wouldn't that be inauthentic? How do I suppose live painting and drumming should look, and where'd those ideas even come from? It feels like the risks of improvising are magnified. And are they greater for M P? Notes melt away, but marks on canvas remain. Left: P+D 01 02 04 (2024); Center: P+D 01 01 03 (2024); Right: P+D 02 02 08 (2024) It's all quite different from watching two musicians improvising. At times they seem at odds, or moving just past one another. Sarin whips himself into a storm, a deluge of creative energy that—in my mind—is an arc of electricity shooting across the stage to directly animate M P's limbs. But Landis is opening a paint bottle or looking for a brush. All that, just dissipated! But has it? I presume bolts of lightning, but am likely missing the charged potential in the air. In some ways, it becomes easier to sense these shifting emotions when there's a visual element, a continuing remnant. In music alone, things often move so quickly that only the most egregious "missteps" or a complete failure to gel create notable feelings of resistance in the witness. Here, things move as fast, but your eyes are drawn to the canvas, which holds on to the movement of the performance like streaks of light in a long exposure. Through all these contours, there's an unmistakable resonance between what Landis and Sarin are doing, if not an equivalence. I feel an immense mental force that wants to draw their activities into a neat consonance, but it's like pushing repelling magnets together. As Landis has always maintained, the painting doesn't "represent" the sounds any more than the reverse. Instead, there's a joyous, if ambiguous, exchange of energy. You can see that it's mutually reinforcing. Sarin is palpably exhilarated. The propulsion of his drumming spurs Landis into action, and the emerging images become mutable graphic scores, giant ever-changing "notes" urging Sarin further. The exact how just evades a tight grasp. Together or separately, the painting and drumming are abstract art that many would accuse of being untethered. But there's something stubbornly literal in their doing. The paintings are just that: caked and layered paint, ink, and pastel, thick and viscous or water-thinned and dripping. The drums: driving, rhythmic, sometimes crashing, deafening, sometimes the faintest texture of hand's skin on drumskin. It is all, plainly, what it is, a frustrating tautology because there is yet, as Sarin said at the end of the most recent performance, an alchemy. "Whole" and "Divided" Painting from Paint & Drums 4, May 9, 2026 at the Loove Annex, Brooklyn, NY Fever Bed To quote another M-P, Maurice Merleau-Ponty wrote in "Cézanne's Doubt" that "before expression, there is nothing but a vague fever, and only the work itself, completed and understood, will prove that there was something rather than nothing to be found there." I'd gently propose shifting the sense of the word "work": M-P wrote l'œuvre , a finished piece of art, an "artifact" of the creative act. I'd like to read it as the doing, le faire, le travail —the undertaking of creating. I often sense that vague fever while listening to improvised music, like the back of my hand against a warm forehead, and admittedly less often when facing a painting. I vicariously feel it in the dim light, watching Landis and Sarin on stage. Still, I sense in myself an inhibiting self-consciousness, like I'd never be able to start, even as I also discover expectations and opinions welling up and fading away as the performance plays out. Once in motion, there's an odd sort of courage in continuing to mark the canvas, to pound the drum, but I wonder if the central task of the improvising artist is to continually overcome that uneasy inertia and just begin . An unstopping at imagination's edge that risks mistake and awkwardness and dissatisfaction to possibly reach something that at best can only be hazily made out, and not at all while sitting in caution and doubt. Unsure if you can know you've reached it. Something about the feeling of reaching. Left: FEVER BED (MAT MANERI TRIO) (2003); Right: manifestation (before fire music) (2001) See much, much more of M P Landis's work, including video clips and other pieces from the Paint & Drums performances, on his Instagram or Facebook pages. items.body: Across eight untitled pieces, fold/interval develops a musical language in which guitar dyads, granular electronics, filtered resonances and microscopic digital artefacts coexist within carefully articulated sonic environments. By directing attention towards the behaviour of sound itself, its texture, spectral balance and the constantly shifting relationships between one resonance and the next, Giuseppe Ielasi and Fabio Perletta engage in an open exchange that is equally balanced and coherent. The title of the project itself offers an illuminating point of entry. In audio synthesis, wavefolding is a process in which a signal exceeding a certain threshold is folded back onto itself, generating new harmonics and increasingly complex timbral structures instead of simply clipping or distorting. The second half of the title is equally revealing. Throughout the album, Giuseppe Ielasi’s guitar is reduced to two-note dyads—musical intervals—whose quiet interjections provide the elementary material from which Fabio Perletta’s electronic processes unfold. Fold describes a continuous process of sonic transformation; interval refers both to the guitar’s harmonic vocabulary and to the spaces separating successive sonic events. The music continually inhabits both meanings. The dialogue between Ielasi and Perletta never feels predetermined. Repeated figures evolve through minute changes in density, frequency and perspective, while silence functions as an active compositional force, shaping every gesture with remarkable precision. Listening gradually shifts away from isolated sonic events towards intervals in both senses of the word: the relationships between pitches and the spaces separating sounds. Tiny overtone fluctuations, delicate feedback and almost imperceptible transients continually redefine the surrounding acoustic field. Giulia Bruno‘s photographic contribution is integral to the project. Her images of landscapes, architectural structures and technological infrastructures mirror the music’s fascination with hidden systems, suspended attention and processes unfolding beneath the threshold of immediate perception. Sound and image share the same temporal logic, encouraging prolonged observation rather than instant recognition. Ultimately, fold/interval is a record about relationships: between acoustic and electronic sound, presence and absence, transformation and stasis. Every gesture appears with an acute sense of proportion. Like the wavefolding process evoked in its title, it reveals how complexity can emerge from the continuous reshaping of the simplest materials. giulia bruno (self portrait giulia bruno) To find out more we have spoken directly with Ielasi, Perletta and Bruno. Untitled (1–8) feels poised between presence and absence: Giuseppe’s sparse guitar gestures seem to emerge from and dissolve back into Fabio’s electronic textures, while Giulia’s photographs introduce a parallel visual rhythm. How did the three of you develop a shared language across sound and image, and at what point did the project become more than a musical collaboration and evolve into fold/interval itself? Giulia Bruno: fold/interval was born from the desire to create together within a free and anti-hierarchical relational context, where sounds and images can also follow a shared path, without subordination. Our relationship began with mutual respect and with a friendship that developed over time. Recognizing ourselves in what each of us does — and perhaps also in who each of us is through our work — created a solid foundation from which the desire emerged to explore something unexpected together, grounded in a shared trust in looking and listening. The project therefore arises from the desire to bring together thoughts, sensibilities, and intuitions that find their form through shared sounds, images, and silences. Fabio Perletta: fold/interval was never just a musical project; rather, it started as a trio. Before that, Giuseppe and I had been discussing the possibility of collaborating in a broader sense. Giulia and Giuseppe already knew each other well, having collaborated for a long time, so everything naturally found its way into fold/interval, which was conceived as a space for exchange involving different practices and sensibilities, where sound and image could develop together. We aim to find a shared space where listening and looking can influence each other, and where unexpected connections could emerge. The music and the photographs are not separate layers, but different manifestations of a shared process and vision. Giuseppe Ielasi: I have been working with Giulia, on different projects, for more than 15 years. This was mainly on film or installation works. More recently we started discussing about possible live performances, and our first one as a duo happened in June 2025 at the Triennale in Milano. We loved it, but at the same time felt the need to work on something less structured, more open to improvisation and surprises. I also know Fabio since a long time: we shared a few concerts and he published some of my music on 901editions, but most of all we exchanged thoughts, music and spent a lot of time together in the last years. We were ready for a collaboration and started playing and recording together. It was very natural, then, to merge those projects, introducing Giulia to Fabio. My impression is that the shared language was already there, it was just a matter of making things happen. fabio perletta (photo oyamada kuniya) The release includes photographs ranging from natural and architectural environments to technological infrastructures, including an image of the cooling systems of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. Given the increasing debate around the environmental cost of AI and large-scale computation, were these infrastructures approached primarily as visual forms, or do they also function as reflections on the invisible systems that increasingly shape contemporary life and knowledge production? GB: My work never approaches images solely as visual forms. Rather, the image is a pretext for activation: a way of bringing to light contemporary questions concerning collective issues, research processes, and systems of relation. In this sense, I am interested in deconstructing the aesthetics of the image, removing it from spectacle so that it can become an activator. An activator of processes of change and reflection on how we observe, recognize, and respond to different forms of violence and contradiction. I believe we are often suspended within a constant tension: between hypnosis and impotence, between beauty and fear, between systems of seduction and power and critical awareness. This is why I am interested in working with the landscape — whether natural, technological, architectural, infrastructural, human, or relational — as a space to be read, questioned, and traversed. The infrastructures, and what is reactivated through photography, are therefore not merely formal presences, but signals of broader, often invisible systems that condition the way we live, know, and imagine the future, within an obsessive system of continuous archiving. To look also means asking ourselves what choices we can make in order to build a collectivity capable of coexisting, resisting, and generating new forms of relation. FP: I believe this connection is at the core of fold/interval. The project does not come from a desire to blindly produce new images and sounds, but rather to create a space where attention can be reactivated and where different, heightened forms of perception coexist. We are not interested in spectacularization, our focus is on cultivating attention. The way we work together is based on a process of listening and waiting, allowing each element to emerge without forcing relationships or creating predetermined correspondences. We were drawn to what happens in the space between things: between the visible and the hidden, between what is heard and what is left in silence. In this sense, fold/interval reflects a resistance to the acceleration and saturation that define contemporary production and consumption. This first work seeks to open up a different temporal dimension—one where the viewer and listener are invited to sit with uncertainty, observe the details, and forge their own connections. giuseppe ielasi (photo philip ielasi) The music is remarkably restrained. Guitar notes and chords seem to drift through digital circuitry, leaving large amounts of space between events. Was reduction a conscious compositional strategy from the outset, or did the pieces gradually arrive at this sparse form through a process of subtraction and editing? FP: From my perspective, it is a combination of both. The way Giuseppe and I approach sound within this project stems from a shared interest in creating an environment where every element holds its own weight and presence, allowing unexpected encounters to unfold. Reduction wasn’t a conscious aesthetic choice; it emerged from a desire to let the space breathe and become an active component of the composition. Silence, resonance, and the intervals between events are not mere voids, but structural pillars that give sounds the room to reveal their intrinsic qualities. At the same time, this sparseness was already baked into the sounds we each brought to the table. Giuseppe’s guitar—with its precision and abstract quality—and my stylized electronic textures, which are often pushed toward the extreme areas of the spectrum, come from very different yet complimentary worlds. Throughout the process, we constantly sought an organic balance between these two worlds, letting the clarity and subtle details of the guitar interact with the ambiguity and roughness of the electronics. GI: It’s strange, the music doesn’t feel that restrained to me. There’s constant activity in it, lots of repetitions (but no loops) and the pacing and placing are very deliberate, but somehow the flow feels very natural (the idea of ‘restrain’ somehow suggest that it was ‘forced’, and that is not the case). There was little subtraction, and almost no editing. We suggested basic materials and layers and realized that many of those could co-exist and interacts very naturally. It was a very intuitive, non-formalised process. Giulia, many of your recent texts engage with questions of technological mediation, the overproduction of images, and the difficulty of maintaining spaces of reflection within contemporary systems of visibility. Do you see a connection between those concerns and the aesthetic choices behind Untitled (1–8), which often feels like it is resisting speed, saturation and information overload in favour of slowness, ambiguity and attention? GB: We are connected by a shared way of thinking: the desire not to follow the logics of production, seduction, and spectacularization, but rather the rhythm of our own thought and listening. It is a natural gaze, made of layers but not oversaturation, of words expressed with care, and of a constant search for coherence. There are no predetermined rules or rigid orders of thought, but rather a natural transformation that emerges from the attempt to remove the work from what is immediately displayed. We are interested in what remains suspended, what requires time, what does not immediately offer itself only as an image or as information. The reflection on the macrosystems in which we move as individuals runs through our thinking and our gaze, and also shapes the way we relate to others. Untitled (1–8) emerges from this attention: from the desire to create a space in which sound, image, and word can slow down perception and open up the possibility of a shared rereading of the processes that involve us. FP: I am drawn to the word Giulia mentioned: rhythm. Our biological rhythm—the intrinsic time we need to process our surroundings—differs for everyone, but it is undeniably a means of survival in this violent, vulgar world. To honor it requires welcoming the complex, the unexpected, the unheard, and the unseen. We aim to stay close to this idea, not in a literal, romantic, or strictly political sense, but as a practice that resists the pressure to produce immediate meaning or visibility. Giulia’s reflection on overproduction and the saturation of images deeply informs how we approach both sound and vision: not as materials to be quickly consumed, but as processes demanding time. The project seeks to create a space where perception can remain open and non-finalised, where things are not immediately resolved into information or representation. Instead, it sustains an alternative internal tempo—one that allows for hesitation, repetition, and return. fold/interval is described not only as an audiovisual project but also as a publishing platform. Beyond this first release, how do you envision the project developing? Are future editions likely to continue exploring the relationship between image, sound and material publication, or do you see fold/interval evolving into a broader framework for collaborations, research projects and new commissions? GB: Starting from the coming together of our conversations, we did not want to place any limit on the project’s transformation. We believe in a path made of coherence, but also of responses to research processes that can change, expand, and take on new forms over time, just as we ourselves change over time. For us, collaboration means first and foremost engaging in dialogue and confrontation. We have not placed any limit on this exchange, except for the desire to do it with people who share with us a vision of the world in which aesthetics is never placed above relationships, research, and the search for meaning in life. In this sense, fold/interval may continue to explore the relationship between image, sound, and material publication, but it may also open itself to other forms: collaborations, research, commissions, dialogues, and processes that have not yet been anticipated. What interests us is that it remains a living space, capable of transforming without losing coherence. FP: For me, fold/interval is less of a fixed container and more of an open ecology, inherently built to evolve. The idea of the publishing platform naturally stems from a desire to give a physical, tangible form to time and thought, which is why the material aspect will always remain a core interest. Looking ahead, I imagine fold/interval evolving as a flexible framework that could manifest as a physical edition, a sound installation, a research residency, or simply a space for shared dialogue. Future editions might not always look or sound the same, it will simply follow the needs of the encounters and questions that emerge along the way. GI: What interests me is to collaborate on a project that’s very open, hard to define and might even be confusing at times. We released an edition with a cd and a set of photos, a short film on our website and we’re co-curating some events and sound installations at “settantaventidue” in Milano. But we also exist as a label / publishing platform (more editions, with or without music, might appear soon and those could include other collaborators) and we’re planning some concerts, residencies and installations for the next months. So, yes, it’s definitely evolving and I’m very curious to see what will happen. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: All in all, a very good introduction to Eighth Tower’s substantial catalog for lovers of deep electronic sound art. Quite recommended while reading Margaret Murray’s acclaimed history of European witchcraft. Related to the occult, divine arts, magic, and the supernatural Witchcraft & Black Magic In The United Kingdom (Expanded Version) by Various Artists   Over the years, the Italian indie label Eighth Tower Records has covered an important amount of themes related to the occult, divine arts, magic, and the supernatural, from historical facts to popular culture (cinema, literature). These topics serve as the conceptual background of many collective releases that feature a number of sound artists from the same family circle (most of them have also published individual releases separately for the label). Titled Witchcraft & Black Magic in United Kingdom, this release is part of the whole concept, but focuses here on witch hunts during the severe repressive years of the Inquisition practiced in a Puritan Anglican Great Britain, notably during the English Civil War. We can remember famous cases during the late medieval and early Renaissance periods, under the cruel activities of Matthew Hopkins toward those accused of renewing a pact with the devil. There is a vast iconography linked to this dark era (Baldung…) and it has also been put on screen a hundred times, as in Witchfinder General, Cry of the Banshee, and Blood on Satan’s Claw. Haunting aural and sonic explorations :: The album is delivered as an extended version of a previous edition released back in 2019. For listeners who are not familiar with this label, it is owned by Raffaele Pezzella (alias Sonologyst), and it has gained a solid reputation over the years thanks to numerous collaborations, reissues… which enrich the field of subterranean dark ambient music and post-industrial sound experimentalism. This version of the album welcomes exclusive tracks by Dead Voices On Air, Mario Lino Stancati and 400 Lonely Things. The musical production embraces haunting aural and sonic explorations, with experimentation on timbres, tone colors, acoustic instrumentation and processed concrete noises. A piece such as “The Village” by the legendary Rapoon is really emblematic of the album, for its soundtrack-like tendency, foggy, echoing acoustic strings and ominous proportions. A personal favorite on this album is the hauntological, ghostly and distorted “Crypt of Saint John” by Howlround. The whole thing is deeply cinematic, evocative, enthralling, abstract and cerebral, with rare moments of suspenseful melodicism. All in all, a very good introduction to Eighth Tower’s substantial catalog for lovers of deep electronic sound art. Quite recommended while reading Margaret Murray’s acclaimed history of European witchcraft. Witchcraft & Black Magic In The United Kingdom (Expanded Version) is available on Eighth Tower. Moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter Such sleek, rhythmic glitch sees rinse.repeat at it again with this oversized extended player, running just over twenty-four minutes and moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter, opening with “ERR_LOOP: Pleasant Failure.” After all this time, its “errors,” under an imprint committed to keeping them “clean,” continue to cultivate minute sonic acrobatics from start to finish. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The inclusion of soprano Marie-Anne Pollaris added a new ingredient to the concoction brewed by Roger Trigaux's band, complementing the King Crimson-esque influences found in the electric guitar work and the atonal piano, courtesy of Alain Rochette. Ferdinand Philippot's bass lines, characterized by the fluid dynamics of jazz-rock fusión, paired seamlessly with Daniel Denis's drumming, which could just as easily support a waltz as it could navigate the most intricate, shifting passages. All of this lends Le poison qui rend fou, Pt. 1: Ram Ram va faire "Pif Paf" its avant-garde flair, evoking an almost cinematic atmosphere, like stepping onto the ledge of an abandoned building, or recalling the dark, modern waltz-like movements found in the Bob Fosse choreography of All That Jazz.When the piano stands alone, it is chamber music... but as the guitar enters while the piano continues, an imperial atmosphere emerges. One imagines that, faced with such a soundscape, the floor simply has to open up and reveal a doorway to another world, which is the concept behind The Poison That Causes Madness.The idea of a modern ballet is actually very fitting, because one can envision a choreography for Ersatz, syncopated, fragmented, broken, dismantled... assembled... and dismantled once more. The piano, the drums, the guitar, they are all disjointed parts that, together, fail to form anything concrete... and yet, within that lack of synchronization, something is found: a message, a breath of life. Another, alternative mode of expression."Le poison qui rend fou, Pt. 2: Didi, dans ta chambre!" presents something circus-like... something pathetic, an old theatrical performance where the protagonists are not up on stage but down below. The dynamic between the electric guitar and the piano is in constant flux, up, down, inducing vertigo; and that is the point: to find no rest, no calm, no refuge. That is the nature of the avant-garde, as someone once said, someone who might well have lost their sanity through such intense contact with art. It is a fire that burns, yet one cannot help but draw near, like insects to a light, while the piano plays on, creating a dense, alarming atmosphere that is decidedly not rock. Urgency is the Word, urgency to speak, to remain silent, but above all to express oneself... in one way or another.An ominous atmosphere ushers in the album's finale with "Samana"; yet, a spirited fusion bassline and atonal piano, vibrant even as the music winds down, embark on a futile quest across a disorienting landscape. Suddenly, calm takes hold, giving way to a suite, an ode to madness. It brings to mind Erasmus of Rotterdam's In Praise of Folly, where stepping outside the boundaries was seen as healthy, as well as Philippe de Broca's film Le Roi de Coeur (1966). All these works speak to the same theme, while piano and guitar trace an invisible line connecting the white of the eye directly to the red of the heart, leaving behind that essential note of unease and intrigue.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A year after forming and recording the Strabismus material in 1972 as well as the initial Riff Raff material (which would not see the light of day until 1999), Roger Sutton is trying again: this time with veterans Peter Kirtley, Tommy Eyre, Brasilian percussionist Aureo De Souza, and Bud Beadle, one of Ian Carr's partners in crime, on saxophones.1. "Your World" (7:39) a gorgeous little 12-string guitar based song with some great vocals from guitarist Peter Kirtley turns to blues-proggy Rock 'n' Roll in the third minute, getting heavier until fully-breaking out into some awesome prog rock in the fourth minute followed by a wonderful slightly-funky Fender Rhodes based Blues-Rock instrumental passage in the fifth over which Peter then turns his significant talent to his electric guitar, delivering an awesome lightly wah-wah-ed solo for almost two minutes. Then the music thins and acoustic guitar and Rhodes rebuild while the lead vocalist ramps things up to reveal a more raspy voice in his impassioned state. But the band softens back up for the final minute, even sporting some gorgeous AMERICA-like harmony vocals to close it out. Wow! I am humbled--and impressed! (14.5/15)2. "For Every Dog" (3:46) a very different version than the one the band had recorded for their original debut record (which never saw the light of day until 1999): this one is much thinner, more stark and open as opposed to the brilliantly layered weaves (both instrumental and vocal) of the original. It's still good but there is no doubt that I prefer the Allan Marshall-fronted version. (8.75/10)3. "Little Miss Drag" (3:12) sounds and plays out like a "new" Beatles tune. Even the sound production is rather like the preferences that John Lennon used in his solo career--even the snarkiness of lyrics have Lennon written all over them! (The songwriting credit cites Sutton and non-members Tony Thorpe and John Richardson as the composers--possibly/probably friends of Roger's.) (8.875/10)4. "Dreaming" (4:32) a two part song that starts out rather innocuously with gentle Fender Rhodes, bass, organ, and cymbal play for the first half minute before Peter's twangy lead electric guitar supplies a Countrified melody before the band cuts back to nothing. Then they slowly build back up while a gentle male vocal sings with an almost insecure vulnerability. Then, at the two-minute mark strummed guitars, jazz piano, hand percussion, and bass launch into a delightfully smooth-yet-spirited two-chord vamp over which Bud's saxophone and Peter's electric guitar play a "solo" melody line as a twin-duo. Really engaging, pretty and fun. (9.25/10)5. "Times Lost" (4:15) another gentle multiple picked acoustic guitar weave with one very gentle, sensitive, almost breathy male voice singing to mimick the Right channel's guitar's treble melody line. I like Roger's fretless bass work here. Nice song though I would never call this Jazz, Rock or even Folk; it's more like acoustic Folk Rock. (9.125/10)6. "You Must Be Joking" (7:29) Jazzy Blues Rock?! Using some DOORS sounds and tricks, the music gradually ramps up into a kind of Jazz-Rock as guitar, keys, and saxophone tracks weave together some pretty intricate riffs and legato lines. Peter Kirtley's lyrics and voice again have an interesting John Lennon-like snark and cleverness while, as said, the Fender Rhodes-based four chord music seems to borrow from The Doors as well as early Who and even Van Morrison. Peter's lead guitar solo in the fourth minute (over some excellent drumming from Aureo) is pretty awesome: definitely deserving of repeated listens and study. (Why did this dude never really make it to the top?) Then comes a stripped down passage within which Tommy Eyre lays down some nice keyboard work with his dirty Rhodes before closing things down by tapering off into . . . silence. (13.75/15)7. "La M�me Chose" (12:12) dreamy Rhodes play with bass, cymbals, and saxophone floating around, trying to figure out their places within the Cosmos. In the third minute Tommy's Rhodes assembles a little momentum, slowly joined by Roger's bass, Aureo's drums, and Peter's rhythm guitar--which eventually become high-tension power chords over which he and the boys sing with some confidence and fire. A slow down in the fifth minute leads into an Allman Brothers-like section, which then ramps back up into the more intense power Folk Rock motif for single- and multiple voice singing. Then, in the seventh minute, things slow back down and thin out with active bass and steady cymbal and rhythm guitar play supporting Tommy's heavily treated Rhodes solo. It's a long solo with every one amping up the further we get into it, but Tommy remaining in the spotlight, taking every second for all he's worth. Bob joins in toward the end to take the volume over the top, causing Tommy to relinquish his lead (and momentum) which then allows Bob a turn in the lead, following the same slow build as they did with Tommy, until guitar power chords take back over as the lead singer returns to declare the song's meaningful intentions before everybody goes into slow decay for the finish. Nice tune! I really love the way the band orchestrates the tension levels throughout--easily and effectively transferring it to we, the listener. (22.5/25)Total Time: 43:05I think it's the prominent acoustic guitars and pleasant, easy-going voices of Roger, Peter, and Tommy that surprise me the most about this album--that and the sophisticated, creative, and confident songwriting.A-/five stars; another minor masterpiece of little-mentioned, perhaps forgotten, song-crafting by some truly excellent and creative songwriters and musicians. Definitely the product of professionals who know what they're doing (and seem to have a strongly defined vision for their music). This may not be as proggy as the Top Tier (mostly symphonic) bands, but it is very high quality music.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — WARNING: This is a release of material recorded in 1972 that represents two different bands containing some of the same musicians that just happen to overlap in that year.Recorded 1972, unreleased until 1999. I was turned on to Riff Raff a few weeks ago so I've been slowly getting to know their music and their story. I was immediately impressed (and astounded that I'd never heard of them--even in my 18 years associated with ProgArchives) by all of their albums--which made the decision of which album to review first very difficult since, in learning their story I'd discovered that their first records--their debut album--had never been released at the time of its creation. But I do like to get to know a band/artist in chronological order if I can, so, of course I want to start with their first album: the problem is that their first album that became known to the public was their second album, the eponymously titled Riff Raff from 1973; Outside Looking In never reached public ears until 1999! As I've been listening to this album I've come to know that the opening 39 minutes represent material performed by the band's original lineup, a project calling themselves, STRABISMUS, which recorded this material in London in 1972. The second 23-minutes of "Bonus Tracks" represents Roger Sutton and Tommy Eyre's more-Jazz-oriented band, RIFF RAFF. Sutton, himself a former member of Brian Auger's Trinity project, continued to develop Riff Raff for the next few years with keyboardist Tommy Eyre, guitarist Peter Kirtley, and drummer Aureo De Souza before giving himself completely to Ian Carr's NUCLEUS. Peter Kirtley's most notable credit post-Riff Raff was his contribution to an album that has always remained dear to me: Yes' Alan White's first solo album, 1976's Ramshackled., while also joining The Pentangle during their tenure in the 1990s. Tommy Eyre himself was a product of previous collaborations with Aynsley Dunbar and Mark-Almond. He would go on to make significant contributions to successful albums by Zzebra, Alex Harvey, Gerry Rafferty, Gary Moore, John Martyn, Greg Lake, Michael Schenker, and Wham!. Singer Alan Marshall was hired by Zzebra (at the suggestion of the band's newcomer keyboard player, Tommy Eyre) as their singer for the 1974-75 sessions and tour that would produce the material for the band's classic sophomore album, Panic, as well as a third and fourth album--which weren't released until 1999 and 2001, respectively. Brasilian-born percussionist/drummer Aureo De Souza would also find himself hired by Ian Carr, as a percussionist, for Nucleus' mid-70s classic funk albums, but the material he recorded with the band never reached the public as part of their studio album releases--only surfaced years later (mostly in the 21st Century) when record labels Vertigo, Andy Gray's BGO (Beat Goes On) Records, and Esoteric Recordings began releasing retrospective CDs that included outtakes and live performances.Line-up / Musicians:As STRABISMUS:- Alan Marshall / vocals- Martin Ball / guitar- Tommy Eyre / Hammond organ, keyboards, acoustic guitar- Richie Dalton / saxophone- Roger Sutton (Brian Auger's Trinity) / bass, acoustic guitars, vocals- Rob Coombes (Juicy Lucy, Stealers Wheel) / drums, percussion & acoustic guitar- Joe Peters (Jackie Jocko) / drumsAs RIFF RAFF:- Alan Marshall / vocals- Peter Kirtley / guitar- Kenny Slade (Joe Cocker) / drums- Aureo De Souza / drums, percussion- Tommy Eyre / Hammond organ, keyboards, acoustic guitar- Richie Dalton / saxophone- Roger Sutton / bass, acoustic guitars, vocals(As Strabismus):1. "Outside Looking In" (9:12) opening a debut album with a long-playing jam is bold and brave! I guess it lets the listener know what kind of band they thought of themselves (unless the song order was altered over time or never decided at the time of its first creation): not hit makers. The material here is heavy, fully Rock 'n' Roll with some creative touches, nice construction and delivery, more akin to hard rockin' guitar-jammin' bands like Cream, Spirit, Mountain, Humble Pie, etc. (18.125/20)2. "The Blind Man" (8:16) opens with a much more acoustic orientation: bluesy piano, percussion and drums, Hammond organ, acoustic guitars, and vocals from a gravelly-voiced male singer. I'm immediately reminded of Southern Rock bands like The Allman Brothers and The Marshall Tucker Band. The cessation of the vocal leads into a rockin' jam with saxophonist Richie Dalton really letting loose with some wild screaming sounds. But then there is this totally unexpected transition around the five-minute mark into a more delicate, almost folk-Mexican acoustic guitar motif in which I believe four of the band members drop their instruments to pick up acoustic guitars and then what sounds like professional choral singers join in singing "Close your eyes, I can feel you" over and over before Alan rejoins to sing over them to the song's close. Very cool and unexpected song and music. (18.25/20)3. "Bach B. Minor Prelude" (2:58) a full solo on a church organ! Luscious! Another very cool and unexpected song. (9/10)4. "Feeling Paranoic" (0:43) a theatric song that feels like an outtake from Judas' or Jesus' performances in Jesus Christ Superstar. (4.375/5)5. "Buthelezi" (3:42) drummer Joe Peters leads the way through a drum & percussion jam that involves Rob Coombes and others. I love this kind of stuff--especially in live performances (or to participate in) but I'm not sure of its place on a studio album: it seems as if this space could/should have been given to a proper full-band song composition. But then I'm beginning to wonder if there is a conceptual theme, intention, or organization to the album. Anyone? (9/10)6. "So You Want To Be Free" (10:52) the music here is a return to the raw hard rock that we encountered with the album's opening song, "Outside Looking In." The raw, gravelly voice of Alan Marshall is back up front for the first couple minutes, then the music transitions into a vamp governed by a quick three-note riff that is repeated over and over while everyone just jams over and around it: saxophone, electric piano, drums, even, eventually, electric guitar. The sax solo is the best of the three; guitarist Martin Ball is not "fully formed" yet though he does sound better once the vamp slows down and punctuates itself like some Swamp Blues and he starts shredding for speed. (I guess he needed to get warmed up.) Martin's solo section ends with some well-timed whole-band chord bashing which sounds really cool and inventive--like something King Crimsonian--but then the music turns to smoother blues rock over which two male vocalists sing, gentler, harmonizing, before the music begins to slowly devolve into just a few percussion/cymbal noises and guitar and electric piano notes. Brilliant--and so creative! (18.25/20)7. "Changes" (3:23) acoustic guitar accompanying Alan's singing on what sounds like a cover but apparently is just another of the album's Sutton/Coombes compositions. Simple and nice; definitely could have been developed into something bigger. (8.667/10)Total time: 39:06A-/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of eclectic Southern Power Rock.Bonus Tracks (as Riff Raff):8. "Child Of The Summer" (5:59) a jazzy feeling song with a syncopated, complex construction and feeling vocal performance (reminiscent of Allan's performance on Allan White's Ramshakled). After the chorus the band revs up and becomes more rock-forceful--but it's still good! Nice wah-wah-ed electric guitar work, great background vocal work, great dirty electric piano, and awesome bass, drums, and percussion at the base. This is the rock-perspective to Jazz-Rock Fusion that I've been hoping to find more of! (9.25/10)9. "For Every Dog" (4:05) a truly awesome acoustic Southern Rock song that should/could've been a radio-friendly hit back in 1973. Great weave of instrumental performances blessed with a weave of awesome group harmonized vocals. Shades of The Youngbloods, Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, Ozark Mountain Daredevils, Pure Prairie League, or the early Doobie Brothers or Eagles. (9.5/10)10. "Morning" (5:57) piano-based soft bluesy light folk/Americana pop arranged with an odd triple-hop at the end of each measure. The singer is mostly backed by another harmonizing vocalist (or vocal track) while acoustic guitars, bass, and gentle drums back/accompany the piano and singers. I believe a flute may also be in the mix though its replication of the piano's legato may be just be a second piano track. A very pleasant, not-quite-Cat Stevens, not-quite-Harry Nilsson tune. (8.875/10)11. "The Garden" (6:59) bluesy solo piano opens this for about 30 seconds before Allan and the background choir vocalists join in. The song sounds almost like a church/liturgical piece--something one might hear in the countryside villages of Ireland. Strummed 12-string acoustic guitar, bass, congas, and drums slowly, almost surreptitiously, join in as Allan gives his hear and soul to his vocal performance. There is definitely a flute in this one--entering just before the piano ramps things up with more volume. There is a little Dave Mason "We Just Disagree" sound and feel here. Then Allan really brings it: belting out with two minutes to go but then things quickly de-escalate as he and his backing singers sing softly about the importance of our ancestor/elders. It drags on a bit but it's a very nice song with a great vocal performance and some nice, positive lyrics. (13.375/15)Total time: 24:00A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Jazz- and Rock-informed Southern Folk Rock.Total Time: 62:06 I don't usually review "bonus" material in my album reviews (because I want to treat the material as it would have been heard in the year it was recorded) but then when this was (finally) released in 1999 it arrived in CD format and, thus, being its first exposure to the public, should be heard as a whole. The problem, of course, comes with the fact that the material is really the result of two completely different bands: one that never really persisted, the other which came out and toured for a year or so before scattering its members across the musical spectrum in the UK and US. I definitely like both "albums" though the Riff Raff "bonus" material is more of the kind of stuff that I'd listen to over and over. (I almost want to rate the two "albums" separately! A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Jazz-infused Southern Folk Rock.

This new project, which already has all 10 songs released on streaming platforms, will now be released as a 180g vinyl record in a super limited edition of only 150 copies.For this new album, in addition to Victor on production and drums, and Lec�o Arroyo on compositions and vocals, a great team of musicians was brought in to take turns recording the tracks. They are: Gui Zucherato, Michel Cury, Marco Kuan, Felipe Prado, Henrique Ucci, Gui Musseli, Fernando Luiz, Jo�o Paulo Martini, Marcel Ziul, Douglas Eurico, Cadu Moreira, Dudu Kanegae, as well as special appearances by Lippo (formerly of Made In Brazil and Harppia), Paulo C�sar Barros (Renato e seus Blue Caps, Raul SEixas and others) and Mario Testoni Jr. (Casa das M�quinas, Rita Lee and Pholhas) The LP that will reach the hands of a select group of fans carries the same DNA of the seventies original rock of the previous album ("70"), featuring Victor Marcellus's striking drumming and the classic sound of the guitars, defining characteristics of Brazilian rock from bands of the 70s, such as Rita Lee and Tutti Frutti, Mutantes, Made in Brazil and Casa das M�quinas.And to achieve this sonic energy, Victor found in musician, singer and songwriter Lec�o Arroyo the perfect partner. Ludwig and Premier drums from the 70s were used in the recordings, as well as original period keyboards such as a tube-powered Hammond L102 from the 1960s.

items.body: Atrición is the sort of record that seems to have been built under fluorescent light, with the smell of disinfectant somewhere nearby and history banging its head against the walls. Santiago Nicolás wrote much of it in an oncology center, and that circumstance hangs over the album with a terrible physical clarity. The body here is material: cells change, systems fail, pressure accumulates, and time works patiently on everything it touches. Nicolás places that fact beside political violence, invasion, borders, archives, and inherited trauma, finding a shared logic in processes that advance by occupation and erosion rather than spectacle. That could have produced a record swollen with significance. Instead, Atrición stays severe, compact, and rhythmically exact. Its drums hit with the blunt economy of DAF and Nitzer Ebb, while the synths carry the cold forward motion of contemporary techno. Suicide lurks in the repetition, Cabaret Voltaire in the sense that machinery can become a social instrument, and Schwefelgelb in the clipped, bodily momentum. Nicolás keeps tightening the screws until repetition stops feeling like recurrence and starts behaving like pressure. This is where the album becomes genuinely nasty in the best sense. A beat returns, a distorted percussion figure acquires another layer, a synthesizer line keeps digging into the same patch of ground, and suddenly you understand accumulation as an experience rather than a concept. Violence, in this framework, survives through systems, habits, documents, buildings, borders, and bodies that continue carrying its consequences after the visible event has passed. Atrición makes persistence feel physical. The lyrics explore themes of archives, silence, trauma, and accountability without resorting to slogans. Nicolás prefers metaphor, allowing the songs to hover between personal memory and public history. His focus is on transmission—what is passed down through generations, what institutions preserve by omission, and what a body retains despite efforts to erase it. The music responds with persistent repetition, reminiscent of bureaucracy but driven by a punchy kick drum. By the end, Atrición feels like a controlled study in pressure: biological, political, historical, rhythmic. Catastrophe often advances by degrees, through small permissions and repeated injuries. He builds music for that recognition, and the result is frightening precisely because it moves with such discipline, until pressure itself becomes its own evidence. Listen to Atrición below and order the EP here. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Nicolás has spent more than a decade moving through electronic music, noise, experimental composition, and post-punk, including work with The Deadly Affair, Access Device, Ángel de la Guarda, and Föllakzoid’s live lineup. Atrición compresses that experience into a language of hard surfaces and accumulating force. The production is clean enough to expose every impact, yet abrasive enough to keep the record from becoming sterile. Follow Santiago Nicolás: Bandcamp Instagram The post Chilean Techno-Industrial Producer Santiago Nicolás Performs an Autopsy on Trauma in “Atrición” EP appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Depeche Mode, the English electronic band from Basildon, Essex, released “Construction Time Again” on 22 August 1983 through Mute Records. The album turns 43 this year. It was the band’s third studio album and reached number 6 on the UK Albums Chart. Daniel Miller produced the album together with Depeche Mode, with Gareth Jones engineering. Recording took place at the Garden studio in London, mixing at Hansa Mischraum in Berlin, and mastering at CBS Studios in London. The band built much of the album around sampled found sounds, recorded on a Synclavier and an Emulator, including metal being struck and other industrial noises. “Construction Time Again” was the first Depeche Mode studio album to feature Alan Wilder as a full member; he co-wrote two of the album’s songs. The nine-track album runs “Love, in Itself,” “More Than a Party,” “Pipeline,” “Everything Counts,” “Two Minute Warning,” “Shame,” “The Landscape Is Changing,” “Told You So” and “And Then…” Mute released “Everything Counts” as the lead single on 11 July 1983, ahead of the album; it reached number 6 on the UK Singles Chart. “Love, in Itself” followed as the second single on 19 September 1983 and peaked at number 21. “Construction Time Again” followed “A Broken Frame” (1982) and preceded “Some Great Reward” (1984), the album that produced “People Are People.” About Depeche Mode Vince Clarke, Martin Gore, Dave Gahan and Andy Fletcher formed Depeche Mode in Basildon, Essex, in 1980, taking their name from a French fashion magazine. The band signed to Daniel Miller’s independent label Mute Records and released the synth-pop debut album “Speak & Spell” in 1981. Clarke left the band after that album to form Yazoo with Alison Moyet, and Gore took over as the band’s main songwriter. Depeche Mode continued as a trio for “A Broken Frame” (1982), then expanded to a four-piece with the addition of Alan Wilder for “Construction Time Again” (1983), the album that introduced sampled industrial sounds and engineer Gareth Jones to the band’s productions. The Miller and Jones production team continued with Depeche Mode through “Some Great Reward” (1984), “Black Celebration” (1986), “Music for the Masses” (1987) and “Violator” (1990), the album that produced “Personal Jesus” and “Enjoy the Silence.” Wilder left the band in 1995 after “Songs of Faith and Devotion” (1993); Depeche Mode continued as a trio of Gahan, Gore and Fletcher, releasing “Ultra” (1997), “Exciter” (2001), “Playing the Angel” (2005), “Sounds of the Universe” (2009), “Delta Machine” (2013) and “Spirit” (2017). Fletcher died in May 2022, and Gahan and Gore released “Memento Mori” as a duo in 2023, touring behind a Mexico City concert film titled “M.” “Construction Time Again,” released 22 August 1983, marked the start of the band’s move from straightforward synth-pop toward the denser, sample-driven productions that shaped its subsequent albums.

items.body: Canadian netlabel Panospria released “I-II-III”, the debut album under the Silver Shadow name, on 15 July 2026. It runs to 26 tracks across three volumes gathered into a single digital set, sold in MP3 and FLAC from 15 Canadian dollars, and it moves between IDM, ambient, drone and minimal techno. The release page presents the album as three distinct volumes compiled into one, and as the latest work of a long-standing name on the label. It never prints that name: “Having recently relocated to France from Canada, keen listeners will surely deduce the identity of this mainstay on our label. New country, new alias, new directions in music.” The label’s own announcement is less coy than the release page. It presents Silver Shadow as the new alias of the artist formerly recording as Silent Q and Gyges. Both of those names belong to Paul Keeley, a Montreal electronic producer whose Gyges album “Composite Massive” was Panospria’s second release in 2004 and who has issued deep and progressive house under his own name through Thinner, Epsilonlab and Anjunadeep. The Silver Shadow Bandcamp page gives the artist’s location as Paris. What is on the Silver Shadow album ‘I-II-III’ The three volumes are not new to the same degree. Volume I is the eight-track album “I”, put on Bandcamp on 26 July 2022, and volume II is the ten-track “II” from 22 November 2024; the remaining eight tracks, from “Delores” to “Matte”, appear here for the first time. II by Silver Shadow Track titles run as compressed fragments throughout: “Aieesqvb96”, “nFU-VHToT”, “HshShsHs”, “HpnoTod”, “Grgwld”, “Dickenszs”. In order the album reads Aieesqvb96, Fulter, Plyurs, nFU-VHToT, Crunge, Duke, Spong, Purf, Ghosnen, AmbWks, Mmoonn, TheLab, Pull, HshShsHs, HpnoTod, Unstld, Grgwld, Roogah, Delores, KiBC8, NewWav, Sheets, Dickenszs, Krud, Thumb and Matte. About Silver Shadow and Panospria Silver Shadow first appeared on Bandcamp on 3 April 2020 with the five-track “A”, followed by “I” in 2022 and “II” in 2024, so the Panospria set is a label debut rather than a first release under the alias. Panospria itself grew out of the Canadian prairies around the turn of the millennium and put out its first offering, the “Alphaform” compilation, in 2002 with Dublin’s Psychonavigation. The label was properly established in Montreal that same year and was among the earliest to treat the MP3 as a release format in its own right. It moved with its operators, running from Montreal until 2008, then Vancouver, then Saskatoon from 2022. Alongside the catalogue it ran two concert series: Textures in Montreal and Quiet City in Vancouver, the latter reaching 70 editions over a decade. In 2007 the Panospria catalogue was folded into the Montreal netlabel No Type, which has been active since 1998 and also runs Annexe, BricoLodge, Nishi and Sine Fiction; Panospria has operated as a No Type sublabel since. Paul Keeley’s connection to the label goes back almost to the start. The Gyges record “Composite Massive” carried the second catalogue number in 2004, and he has since appeared on Panospria releases by Heart & Soul, Shoebomber, Arnau Sala and N4K3D D1G1TS. “I-II-III” is the first Silver Shadow release Panospria has issued, and by the label’s account the first since the move from Canada to France.

items.body: German EBM and electro label emmobiz records releases “V.A. 19. Elektrisch Festival” on 24 October 2026, the same day as the 19th Elektrisch Festival at Club Seilerstraße in Zwickau. The 10-inch is pressed on brown vinyl, limited to 222 copies, and sells for 16.99 euro through the label’s own shop. Six tracks from five acts fill the two sides. The record continues an annual series that the label has run since the festival returned in 2024, following the red-vinyl 16th edition and the 17th edition 10-inch, and the 18th, which split across an EBM Edition and a Synth Pop Edition earlier this year. emmobiz describes the Elektrisch series as the only festival compilation of its kind carrying rare or exclusive tracks from the acts on the bill. What is on the 19. Elektrisch Festival 10-inch Four of the five acts on the record play the festival. Portion Control, this year’s headliner, does not appear on the compilation. The label fills the gap with two bonus tracks by acts outside the bill. A1: Escalator, “Utolsókor (Short)”, 3:47 A2: Oszylayter, “we’re the noise”, 4:01 A3: Cyborg Projekt X, “Native Terror” (Vinyl Edit), 3:49 B1: Krieg-B, “kill the light” (V111 Mix), 5:20 B2: Sabotage Q.C.Q.C., “Heidenangst” (Drumatic), 6:05 B3: TöT, “Diers Irae” (Rough Mix), 2:27 The two bonus cuts on the B-side reach outside the festival line-up. Sabotage Q.C.Q.C. are a German electro act who released through Spin Records and EMI Electrola in the 1990s; “Heidenangst” first appeared on their 1996 album “Sexploitation Cinema” and returned in remixed form on the 1997 maxi-single “Schlager”. The version here is a new remake made for this record. Closing the compilation, the Marseille electro-punk and EBM band TöT contribute “Diers Irae”. Escalator, the Budapest EBM band founded in 1988 by 2RT+TB, took their starting point from Kraftwerk and have released since 1989. Oszylayter bring electropunk and breakbeat from Germany. Krieg-B, the Franco-Belgian project Dominique Lallement and Benoît Buyse started in June 2023, follow their emmobiz debut “War Drums’ Resonance” with the album “Concrete Dominion”, which the label also dates to 24 October. About the Elektrisch Festival and emmobiz records The Elektrisch Festival ran five editions in Zwickau between 2007 and 2010, from the 11th to the 15th, at the city’s BPM Club. It then stopped for 14 years. emmobiz records brought it back in 2024 with the 16th edition at Club Seilerstraße, which sold out in advance behind Calva Y Nada, Cat Rapes Dog, Digital Factor and Accessory. The 17th followed in October 2025 and the 18th ran over two evenings in February 2026. The 19th takes place on 24 October 2026 with Portion Control, Escalator, Oszylayter, Cyborg Projekt X and Krieg-B; doors open at 19:00 and the music starts at 20:00. emmobiz records is run by Jörg Freier from Oelsnitz in the Erzgebirge, Saxony, and specialises in industrial, EBM and synthpop. The label stopped operating at the end of 2017 and relaunched on 22 August 2024 with a vinyl reissue of Tyske Ludder’s “Bombt Die Mörder?”. Since then it has reissued the Calva Y Nada catalogue on picture disc, pressed Apoptygma Berzerk’s “Kathy’s Song XXV”, and put out records by Second Decay, Blind Passengers, Fairlight Children and Piston Damp. It organises the festival as well as documenting it, and the 10-inch goes on sale the day the doors open.
